name: Israeli Single Malt
description: Whisky matured in Tel Aviv's heat and humidity, where a cask loses far more each year than in Scotland and the spirit comes of age in a fraction of the time. Milk & Honey opened the category in 2012.
funFact: Some casks mature in warehouses near the Dead Sea, the lowest point on land, where the air pressure and heat push maturation faster still.

serve.how: Neat, with a few drops of water. Rapid tropical maturation means young whisky here carries heavy wood, so water helps pull the spirit back out from under it.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in Israel's Mediterranean climate.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, sherry, wine and pomegranate casks; three years and up

composition.process: Annual evaporation runs several times the Scottish rate, which concentrates the spirit fast.

name: Sabra
description: Israeli chocolate and Jaffa orange liqueur, launched in the 1960s in a bottle modelled on an ancient Phoenician oil flask. Sweet, dark, and named after the prickly pear as a nickname for native-born Israelis.
funFact: The bottle shape was based on a two-thousand-year-old Phoenician vessel, and the design was commissioned specifically to look archaeological.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice. It also works poured over ice cream and stirred into coffee. Very sweet, so a small measure is enough.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with chocolate and Jaffa orange.
composition.process: Jaffa oranges were Israel's signature export crop, which is what tied the liqueur to national identity.

name: Aragh Sagi
description: Iranian raisin spirit, distilled illicitly since the 1979 revolution made alcohol illegal. The name translates as dog sweat, which is either self-deprecating humour or an accurate description depending on the batch.
funFact: Iran has one of the world's oldest winemaking traditions, with evidence of grape fermentation in the Zagros mountains going back seven thousand years.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, and privately. Quality ranges from carefully double-distilled to genuinely dangerous, and methanol poisoning from bad batches is a recurring problem in Iran.

composition.summary: Raisins fermented and distilled in home stills.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Homemade stills, single or double distillation

composition.process: Raisins are legal to buy in quantity, which is precisely why they became the base.

name: Indian Molasses Whisky
description: The overwhelming majority of what India calls whisky is distilled from molasses rather than grain, which means most of the world's best-selling whisky brands are not whisky under European law at all.
funFact: Several Indian brands sell more cases annually than the entire Scotch whisky industry, purely on the strength of the domestic market.

serve.how: With soda and ice, which is how India drinks it, or with water. It is sweeter and lighter than grain whisky and is built for long mixing rather than neat contemplation.

composition.summary: Molasses spirit blended with a small proportion of malt whisky.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, usually with some malt whisky blended in

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often minimal; tropical maturation is fast

composition.process: India taxes and defines whisky domestically, which is why molasses-based spirit can carry the name there.

name: Coconut Feni
description: The other Goan feni, distilled from coconut palm toddy rather than cashew apples. Older than the cashew version, since cashews only arrived with the Portuguese, and now much the rarer of the two.
funFact: Toddy tappers climb the palms twice daily and are a vanishing profession in Goa, which is the main reason coconut feni is disappearing.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or with lime soda, which is the standard Goan serve. It is funkier and more savoury than cashew feni, and it takes acid well.

composition.summary: Coconut palm sap fermented and pot-distilled in stages.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Toddy tapped from coconut palm flower stalks

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional pot distillation, typically three runs

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; some rest in earthenware

composition.process: The sap ferments within hours of tapping, so distillation happens the same day.

name: Mahua
description: Distilled from the flowers of the mahua tree, which fall in spring and are gathered by Adivasi communities across central India. Long dismissed as country liquor, it was reclassified as heritage liquor in 2021.
funFact: Mahua flowers are also eaten and used as a sweetener, and the tree is treated as sacred in several Adivasi traditions.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass. The flavour is floral and strange, closer to a fortified honey than to anything grain-based. The new commercial bottlings are considerably cleaner than the village versions.

composition.summary: Dried mahua flowers fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Flowers of Madhuca longifolia, gathered as they fall

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional clay or pot stills; modern producers use copper

composition.process: The flowers are naturally high in sugar and need no addition to ferment.

name: Indian Rum
description: Dark, sweet and heavily molasses-driven, of which Old Monk is the icon: a vatted seven-year rum that built a cult following without ever advertising. India drinks an enormous amount of it.
funFact: Old Monk was famously never advertised, relying entirely on word of mouth, and for decades it was among the best-selling dark rums in the world.

serve.how: Neat, over ice, or with cola. Indian winters call for it hot with water and honey. It is sweet and vanilla-forward, so it does not need much help.

composition.summary: Sugarcane molasses fermented, distilled and aged in the Indian climate.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, tropically matured; Old Monk is vatted at seven years

composition.process: India grows more sugarcane than almost anywhere, so molasses has always been the obvious base.

name: Tharra
description: Sugarcane moonshine from the northern Indian plains, distilled from fermented cane juice or jaggery in village stills. Illegal, widespread, and the subject of periodic poisoning tragedies when batches are adulterated.
funFact: Mass poisonings from methanol-adulterated country liquor remain a recurring public health emergency across northern India.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and only from a source you trust absolutely. This is one of the entries on this list where the safety caveat is not a formality.

composition.summary: Cane juice or jaggery fermented and distilled in improvised stills.
composition.process: Adulteration with industrial methanol to boost strength is the cause of most tharra fatalities.

name: Indian Gin
description: A genuinely new category: gins built on Indian botanicals — Goan coriander, Himalayan juniper, gondhoraj lime, black pepper from Kerala. India had no craft gin at all before 2017 and now exports it.
funFact: India grows a large share of the world's spices, so the botanical supply chain that most gin producers import from was already domestic.

serve.how: With a light tonic and a wedge of lime or a few crushed pink peppercorns. The spice-forward botanicals are strong enough that a heavily flavoured tonic will bury them.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with Indian and Himalayan botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Himalayan juniper, gondhoraj lime, coriander, pepper, fennel, cardamom

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour infusion

composition.process: Sourcing juniper from the Himalayas rather than Europe is what several producers use to define the category.

name: Ceylon Arrack
description: Sri Lanka's national spirit, distilled from the fermented sap of coconut flowers and rested in halmilla wood. Light, faintly funky and closer to a soft rum than to anything else, and quite unlike Batavia arrack.
funFact: Toddy tappers move between palm crowns on ropes strung fifteen metres above the ground rather than climbing down between trees.

serve.how: With ginger beer and lime, which is the Sri Lankan standard, or over ice with soda. The premium aged bottlings are worth drinking neat, where the halmilla wood shows as a soft spice.

composition.summary: Coconut flower sap fermented and distilled, then aged in halmilla casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Toddy from coconut palm flower stalks

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Halmilla wood vats, six months to fifteen years

composition.process: The sap must be distilled within a day of tapping, since it ferments almost immediately in the heat.

name: Kasippu
description: Sri Lanka's illicit moonshine, distilled from sugar, cane or fermented fruit in the countryside, and by some estimates outselling every licensed spirit on the island combined.
funFact: Estimates of unlicensed alcohol in Sri Lanka regularly put it at over half of all consumption, most of it kasippu.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, from a source you know. It is produced entirely outside regulation and is frequently adulterated, which makes it a genuine risk rather than a novelty.

composition.summary: Sugar, cane or fruit fermented and distilled in hidden stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugar, cane juice or fermented fruit

composition.process: Production is deliberately mobile, since the stills have to be moved to avoid enforcement.

name: Raksi
description: Nepali millet or rice spirit, distilled at home in stacked clay or metal pots and served warm in the hills. Cloudy, sour and warming, and offered at every festival and family occasion.
funFact: The traditional still is a stack of pots with a cold-water bowl on top, and the condensate is caught in a vessel suspended inside.

serve.how: Served warm, often with a piece of fried egg or meat floated on top at festivals. Strength varies wildly between households, so the first cup is a reasonable guide to pacing.

composition.summary: Millet or rice fermented with a starter cake and pot-distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Stacked pot still over an open fire

composition.process: Marcha carries both the yeast and the moulds that convert the grain's starch to sugar.

name: Aila
description: The Newar community's rice spirit, distilled in Kathmandu valley courtyards and central to Newari feasts. Traditionally poured from a clay jug into a leaf cup, and drunk as part of ritual as much as celebration.
funFact: At certain Newari festivals aila is poured directly into the mouth from a clay jug held above the head, without touching the lips.

serve.how: Room temperature or gently warmed, as part of a Newari feast rather than on its own. The first distillate, called thaha, is the strongest and is kept for elders and guests.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a yeast starter and distilled in traditional stills.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Stacked clay or copper pot still

composition.process: Successive fractions are collected separately, and the first is prized well above the rest.

name: Ara
description: Bhutan's home-distilled spirit, made from rice, maize, millet or wheat and served hot with butter and a scrambled egg dropped in. That version, called hoentay ara, is a genuine winter staple.
funFact: Commercial production and sale is restricted in Bhutan, so nearly all ara is made at home for family and guests.

serve.how: Heated with butter and a beaten egg stirred through, which sounds alarming and is genuinely good at altitude in winter. Also drunk cold and plain, though far less often.

composition.summary: Grain fermented with a local starter and distilled at home.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Simple pot still over a stove

composition.process: Butter and egg are added at serving rather than in production, and the fat carries the warmth.

name: Murree
description: Pakistan's only legal distillery, founded in 1860 to supply the British garrison and still operating in an Islamic republic where most citizens cannot legally buy its products.
funFact: Murree cannot export easily and cannot sell to Muslim Pakistanis, so it operates in one of the strangest commercial positions of any distillery on earth.

serve.how: Neat or with a splash of water. The older single malts are genuinely accomplished and comparable to mid-range Scotch, which surprises almost everyone who tries one.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in Pakistan.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and sherry oak, eight to twenty-one years

composition.process: The brewery and distillery survived partition, prohibition and nationalisation by continuing to operate under licence.

name: Bangla Mod
description: Bangladesh's licensed country liquor, distilled from molasses or rice and sold through a small number of permitted outlets. Cheap, strong, and a rare legal product in a country with very tight alcohol laws.
funFact: Bangladesh requires a permit to buy alcohol legally, and country liquor shops operate under a licensing system inherited from colonial administration.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures. It is a functional spirit rather than a refined one, and the licensed version is considerably safer than the unlicensed alternatives circulating alongside it.

composition.summary: Molasses or rice fermented and distilled under licence.
composition.process: The licensed trade exists partly to displace the far more dangerous informal one.

name: Uzbek Konyak
description: Central Asian brandy made in the Soviet style from grapes grown in the Ferghana valley and around Samarkand. Sweeter and softer than French brandy, and a legacy of Soviet-era winemaking on the Silk Road.
funFact: The Soviet Union built a substantial brandy industry across Central Asia and the Caucasus, and konyak remains the standard local word for it.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, usually with a meal rather than after it, as is the custom across the former Soviet republics. Frequently accompanied by more toasts than is strictly advisable.

composition.summary: Uzbek wine distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grapes from the Ferghana valley and Samarkand region

composition.process: Hot continental summers give very ripe grapes, which is why the resulting brandy runs sweet.

name: Sauce-Aroma Baijiu
description: The jiangxiang style, from Guizhou, and the most expensive baijiu made. Fermented and distilled seven times over a year, it tastes of soy sauce, mushroom and dried meat rather than anything a Western palate calls a spirit.
funFact: The production cycle runs a full year with nine steamings, eight fermentations and seven distillations, and the spirit is then aged for at least three more.

serve.how: Room temperature in a very small cup, with food, and shared. Chinese banquet custom is to toast rather than sip. The umami depth needs food alongside it; drunk alone it can be overwhelming.

composition.summary: Sorghum solid-state fermented with wheat qu in stone pits, distilled seven times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Red sorghum and wheat qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Seven distillations across a year-long cycle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware jars, then blended

composition.process: 53% is considered the point where water and ethanol molecules bind most tightly, and the style is bottled there deliberately.

name: Strong-Aroma Baijiu
description: The nongxiang style from Sichuan, fermented in mud pits that have been in continuous use for centuries and are treated as the distillery's most valuable asset. Pungent, fruity and enormously popular.
funFact: Luzhou Laojiao's oldest fermentation pits date from 1573 and have been running without interruption since, with the microbial culture in the mud considered irreplaceable.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with food. The fruit-and-funk profile is intense on its own but cuts through rich, oily Sichuan food remarkably well. Toast rather than sip.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in aged mud pits, distilled and blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with rice, wheat, corn and glutinous rice

composition.process: The older the mud pit, the more complex the microbial population, and the higher the value of the spirit.

name: Light-Aroma Baijiu
description: The qingxiang style from Shanxi, fermented in stone jars rather than earth pits, which keeps it clean and floral. The most approachable baijiu for anyone new to the category, and the historical ancestor of Korean soju.
funFact: Fenjiu from Xinghua village is documented as far back as the Northern and Southern dynasties, making it one of the oldest named spirits in China.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food, or lightly chilled if it is your first baijiu. Its cleaner profile also makes it the style most usable in cocktails, where it behaves a little like a funky gin.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in stone jars with barley and pea qu.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, with a barley and pea qu starter

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware, typically shorter than other styles

composition.process: Stone jars keep the ferment isolated from soil microbes, which is why the style stays clean.

name: Rice-Aroma Baijiu
description: The mixiang style from Guangxi and southern China, distilled from rice rather than sorghum. The lightest and most delicate of the four classic aromas, and the closest baijiu gets to a soft, sweet spirit.
funFact: Sanhua jiu from Guilin is the best-known example and is traditionally aged in caves cut into the karst hills around the city.

serve.how: Room temperature or lightly chilled, in small cups. It is gentle enough to drink without food, which is unusual for baijiu, and it works well alongside lighter southern Chinese cooking.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a small qu starter and distilled.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars, sometimes in karst caves

composition.process: A smaller qu starter than the northern styles means less funk and more of the rice.

name: Erguotou
description: Beijing's everyday baijiu, cheap, clean and sold in a small green bottle that costs less than a bowl of noodles. The name means second pot head, referring to the middle fraction of the distillation that goes into it.
glassware: Small cup or straight from the bottle
funFact: The little green bottle of Red Star erguotou is such a Beijing fixture that it has become a design shorthand for the city itself.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with street food. It is a working drink and treated as one; nobody in Beijing contemplates their erguotou. It also mixes surprisingly well with sour or citrus flavours.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented and distilled, with only the middle cut kept.
composition.process: Discarding the head and tail of the run is exactly what the name describes, and why it is cleaner than its price suggests.

name: Mei Kuei Lu Chiew
description: Baijiu infused with rose petals and rock sugar, used at least as often in Chinese kitchens as in glasses. It flavours char siu and roast meats, and quietly does the work in a great many restaurant dishes.
funFact: It is a standard ingredient in Cantonese roast meat marinades, where the rose note is barely detectable in the finished dish but its absence is.

serve.how: Neat in a small cup, though most bottles go into cooking. In the glass it is intensely floral and strong; a very small measure is enough. It also makes an interesting cocktail modifier.

composition.summary: Sorghum baijiu infused with rose petals and rock sugar.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dried rose petals and rock sugar

composition.process: The high strength is what makes it useful in cooking, since it carries flavour into fat and burns off cleanly.

name: Yaojiu
description: Chinese medicinal liquor, made by steeping herbs, roots, ginseng, deer antler or whole snakes in baijiu. Prescribed rather than ordered, and drunk in small measures for specific complaints.
funFact: Snake wine, in which a whole venomous snake is submerged in spirit, relies on the alcohol denaturing the venom, which it does.

serve.how: A small measure, taken deliberately rather than socially. Traditional Chinese medicine assigns different preparations to different conditions, and it is drunk in that spirit rather than for pleasure.

composition.summary: Baijiu steeped with medicinal herbs, roots or animal ingredients.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ginseng, goji, deer antler, snake, wolfberry, dozens of herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, often for months or years

composition.process: High-strength spirit is used because it extracts compounds that water cannot.

name: Kaoliang
description: Sorghum spirit from Kinmen, a Taiwanese island a few kilometres off the Chinese mainland, distilled in tunnels dug during the artillery bombardments of the 1950s. Bottled at 58% and drunk with real ceremony.
funFact: The distillery was founded in 1952 to give the garrison something to make from local sorghum, and it became Kinmen's principal industry.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. At 58% it is not a sipping spirit; Taiwanese custom is to drain the cup on a toast and refill.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented with wheat qu and solid-state distilled.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Stored in granite tunnels cut into the island

composition.process: The granite tunnels hold a stable cool temperature year-round, which is why they are still used.

name: Imo Shochu
description: Sweet potato shochu from Kagoshima, earthy and unmistakable, with a heavy aroma that divides opinion even within Japan. Single-distilled at low pressure to keep the character rather than strip it.
funFact: Kagoshima's volcanic soil is poor for rice but ideal for sweet potato, which is why the region distils rather than brews.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

name: Mugi Shochu
description: Barley shochu, most of it from Oita, and the gentlest of the styles. Clean and lightly nutty, and the usual recommendation for anyone meeting shochu for the first time.
funFact: Iki island in Nagasaki holds a geographical indication for barley shochu and claims to have originated the style in the sixteenth century.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with cold water
serve.how: On the rocks, or mizuwari with cold water at about one to one. Barrel-aged versions drink comfortably neat and are often mistaken for a light whisky in a blind pour.

composition.summary: Barley fermented with barley koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, often under vacuum for a lighter result

composition.process: Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point and produces a markedly cleaner, fruitier spirit.

name: Kome Shochu
description: Rice shochu, the closest the category comes to sake in flavour, and concentrated in Kumamoto's Hitoyoshi basin where it holds a geographical indication. Soft, floral and quietly excellent.
funFact: Kuma shochu from the Hitoyoshi basin is one of only a handful of Japanese spirits with a protected geographical indication.

serve.temp: room temp, warm or on the rocks
serve.glass: Wine glass, or warmed in a choku
serve.how: Warmed gently in winter, on the rocks in summer, or neat at room temperature. Kuma shochu is traditionally pre-mixed with water and warmed in a ceramic flask overnight before serving.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.
composition.process: Both the base and the koji are rice, which is why it sits so close to sake on the palate.

name: Kokuto Shochu
description: Brown sugar shochu, made only on the Amami islands between Kyushu and Okinawa, where a post-war tax arrangement granted the exclusive right to produce it. Nowhere else in Japan may legally make it.
funFact: Amami's exclusive right dates from the islands' return to Japan in 1953, when the arrangement was made to protect the local sugar economy.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with water
serve.how: On the rocks, or with cold water. Despite the base it is not sweet, since the sugar ferments out entirely. It sits somewhere between a light rum and a shochu, which is exactly what it is.

composition.summary: Brown sugar fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji, which is legally required

composition.process: The rice koji requirement is what keeps it classified as shochu rather than as rum.

name: Japanese Gin
description: Gin built on Japanese botanicals — yuzu, sansho pepper, sencha, hinoki cypress, shiso — and distilled with the precision the country brings to everything else. A category that did not meaningfully exist before 2016.
funFact: Ki No Bi separates its botanicals into six groups and distils each separately before blending, which is closer to perfumery than to conventional gin-making.

serve.how: A Japanese-style highball with soda and a twist of yuzu or lemon, built in a tall glass with hard clear ice. Tonic works but is heavy-handed against sencha and sansho, which are easily lost.

composition.summary: Rice or grain spirit redistilled with Japanese botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice spirit or neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, yuzu, sansho, sencha, gyokuro, hinoki, shiso, ginger

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Often distilled in separate botanical groups, then blended

composition.process: A rice spirit base is softer and slightly sweeter than grain, which suits the delicate botanicals.

name: Andong Soju
description: Traditional distilled soju from Andong, made from rice and nuruk at around 45%, and a completely different drink from the diluted green-bottle soju that dominates Korean sales. Designated an intangible cultural property.
funFact: Distilled soju arrived in Korea with the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century, and Andong was one of the garrison towns where the technique took root.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with nuruk and distilled in a traditional soju gori.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in an earthenware soju gori

composition.process: Nuruk carries a wilder mix of moulds and yeasts than Japanese koji, which gives a more rustic result.

name: Insamju
description: Korean ginseng liquor, with whole roots visible in the bottle, made by steeping ginseng in distilled soju. Taken as a tonic as much as a drink, and given as a gift at least as often as it is opened.
funFact: Korean red ginseng is graded and priced by shape as well as age, and roots resembling a human figure command a substantial premium.

serve.how: A small measure, room temperature, usually with a meal. Koreans treat it as restorative rather than recreational, and it appears at gatherings for older relatives more than young ones.

composition.summary: Distilled soju steeped with whole ginseng root.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Korean ginseng, often with jujube and honey

composition.process: Six-year-old red ginseng is the prized grade, and it keeps infusing in the bottle.

name: Korean Whisky
description: Korea released its first domestic single malt in 2023, matured through summers that swing far hotter and winters far colder than Scotland's. The extreme range pushes the spirit through wood at speed.
funFact: Ki One, from a distillery outside Namyangju, released Korea's first single malt after fewer than three years of maturation, which the climate made possible.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. These are young whiskies matured fast, so the wood arrives early and water helps separate it from the spirit. Cask-strength releases benefit most.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in Korea's continental climate.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and sherry casks, three years and up

composition.process: Summers above 35°C and winters below freezing drive the spirit in and out of the wood each year.

name: Arkhi
description: Mongolian spirit distilled from fermented mare's or cow's milk, made on the steppe in a wooden column set over the stove. Cloudy, sour and low in strength, and utterly unlike anything else distilled anywhere.
funFact: It is distilled from airag, fermented mare's milk, and the distilling apparatus sits directly on the family stove inside the ger.

serve.how: Served warm in a small bowl, offered with the right hand, and accepted with both. Refusing outright is impolite; touching it to your lips and returning it is not. Strength is low, so several rounds are normal.

composition.summary: Fermented milk distilled in a stovetop wooden column.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Airag, fermented mare's milk, or cow's milk

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Wooden column still set over the ger stove

composition.process: Milk sugar is what ferments here rather than starch or fruit sugar, which is why nothing else tastes like it.
